title: Moses in Akiva's class (Menachot 29b)
hookLine: Moses sits in Akiva's class and can't follow, until Akiva says "this is from Moses at Sinai"
tomorrow: the Torah says Moses died "by the mouth" of God. meaning what?

cards: Somewhere there's a card or a recipe in an older relative's handwriting. Look at the letters, not the words: the loops, the slant, the little flicks at the top.

In a Torah scroll, some Hebrew letters wear tiny strokes on top, like crowns. The Talmud has a story that starts with those crowns, and ends with Moses himself sitting in the back of a classroom, lost.

teach.h: GOD TIES CROWNS ON THE LETTERS.
teach.b: When Moses goes up to receive the Torah, the Talmud says, he finds God tying little crowns onto the letters. He asks why.
God answers: generations from now there will be a man named Akiva, who will draw heaps and heaps of teachings out of every one of these strokes. Moses asks to see him. God says: turn around.
Suddenly he's seated behind eight rows of students in Rabbi Akiva's class. And he can't follow. They're discussing his own Torah, and he doesn't recognize it, and his strength fails him.
The room is full of questions he never asked. Then a student asks: Rabbi, how do you know this?
Akiva answers: it's a law given to Moses at Sinai. And Moses' mind is put at ease.

Here's one to tell a friend tonight: in this story, Moses himself is lost in a class about the Torah he received, and he's comforted when he hears his own name. The tradition holds two things at once.
It grows, stroke by stroke, past what its first teacher could picture.

teach.h: IT GROWS AND NAMES THE ROOT.
teach.b: And every new branch still names the root.
Growth here isn't betrayal. It's a living tradition saying where it came from.

how: Torah scrolls are written by hand by a trained scribe, and certain letters carry small crowns (tagin). Jewish study often traces a later teaching back through its chain of teachers to Sinai.

games.q: your little cousin asks why your family sings songs at the Hanukkah candles that your great-grandparents never sang. by the story, what's a good answer?
o: the tradition grows, and every new branch still comes from the same root.
those songs don't really count, since they weren't there at the start.
nothing has ever changed; it's exactly how it was always done.
games.why: Moses couldn't follow Akiva's class, yet Akiva named Moses at Sinai as the source. growth and roots go together.

practice: Find any page near you: a book, a label, your own notes. Choose one letter and look at it closely, where the stroke starts, where it bends, the little flick at the top.

Now trace it slowly with a fingertip, on the page or in the air, as if you were adding a crown. Someone taught you that shape, and someone taught them; keep tracing, slowly, for the length of the sit.

wordCard.voice: Moses in Akiva's class: the Talmud's story of the tradition growing past its first teacher, and still calling him its root.

orig.note: Hebrew: crowns. in the story, God ties crowns onto the letters of the Torah.

carryVoice: Remember: moses couldn't follow, and it was still his Torah. Thirty-three of forty in the block.

sources.ref: Babylonian Talmud, Menachot 29b (God ties crowns on the letters; Moses sits behind eight rows in Akiva's study house; 'a law given to Moses at Sinai')
